content: Thiram, also known as tetramethylthiuram disulfide, is an ectoparasiticide. It is primarily utilized to prevent fungal diseases in seeds and crops. Additionally, it serves as an animal repellent, protecting fruit trees and ornamental plants from damage caused by rabbits, rodents, and deer. Thiram is effective against various plant diseases, including stem gall of coriander, damping-off, smut of millet, and neck rot of onion. Historically, it has also been employed in the treatment of human scabies, as a sunscreen, and as a bactericide applied directly to the skin or incorporated into soap formulations. Thiram is classified as a sulfur-based fungicide. It is completely soluble in solvents such as chloroform, acetone, and ether. It is available in various formulations, including dust, flowable concentrates, wettable powders, water-dispersible granules, and water suspension formulations. It is also often combined with other fungicides. In soil, thiram exhibits low mobility, particularly in clay soils or soils with high organic matter content. Due to its in-soil half-life of approximately 15 days and its strong tendency to adhere to soil particles, it is not expected to contaminate groundwater. Thiram exhibits moderate toxicity when ingested but is highly toxic if inhaled. Acute exposure in humans can result in symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal disturbances. It is known to irritate the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract and acts as a skin sensitizer. Symptoms of acute inhalation exposure include itching, a scratchy throat, hoarseness, sneezing, coughing, nasal or throat inflammation, bronchitis, dizziness, headaches, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal complaints. Individuals with pre-existing chronic respiratory or skin conditions are at an increased risk of adverse effects from thiram exposure. Chronic exposure to thiram can lead to additional symptoms beyond those associated with acute exposure. These include drowsiness, confusion, loss of libido, incoordination, slurred speech, and generalized weakness. Prolonged or repeated exposure may also result in allergic reactions, such as dermatitis, watery eyes, sensitivity to light, and conjunctivitis.
